mcqs.q: The ALARA principle stands for:
mcqs.explain: ALARA = As Low As Reasonably Achievable — because even a small dose may cause a stochastic effect, exposure is always minimized.

mcqs.q: Approximately what fraction of the population's radiation dose comes from NATURAL sources?
mcqs.explain: About 83% of population dose is natural (cosmic, terrestrial, radon, food) and ~17% is artificial (mainly medical).

mcqs.q: Which is an INTERNAL natural source of background radiation?
mcqs.explain: Radon and its progeny are the main internal natural source; cosmic and terrestrial radiation are external natural sources.

mcqs.q: In dental radiology, radiation emitted by parts of the x-ray tube OTHER than the focal spot is called:
mcqs.explain: Leakage = radiation from any tube part other than the focal spot. The primary beam comes from the focal spot; scatter comes from matter the beam passes through.

mcqs.q: Radiation emitted by the substance (patient tissues) through which the x-rays pass is:
mcqs.explain: Secondary/scattered radiation is produced within the matter the beam passes through — the main source of dose to the operator.

mcqs.q: The ICRP and NCRP are bodies that:
opts: Set radiation-protection standards without unduly limiting beneficial uses
mcqs.explain: ICRP (International) and NCRP (National) Commissions on Radiation Protection set protection standards, aiming to protect people without unduly limiting beneficial practices.

mcqs.q: Radiographs should be prescribed:
opts: Only after clinical examination and professional judgment — never as a substitute for it
Routinely for every patient before any examination
At fixed intervals regardless of need
mcqs.explain: Patient selection: radiographs follow clinical examination and professional judgment; they supplement, never replace, clinical assessment.

mcqs.q: Among intra-oral film speed groups D, E and F:
opts: F is the fastest and needs the least exposure (lowest dose)
D is the fastest and needs the least exposure
Slower film gives the lowest dose
mcqs.explain: Speed increases D → E → F (each ~2× faster). Faster film needs less exposure time, lowering dose (with a slight loss of image quality).

mcqs.q: Rare-earth intensifying screens (panoramic/cephalometric) reduce radiation exposure by about:
mcqs.explain: A rare-earth screen + film combination reduces exposure by ~55%. Gadolinium/lanthanum emit green light; calcium tungstate emits blue.

mcqs.q: Increasing the focal-spot-to-film distance (long FSFD) reduces patient exposure by about ___ and also:
opts: 32%; gives a less divergent beam and better resolution
mcqs.explain: A long FSFD reduces exposure ~32%, makes the beam less divergent and improves resolution; the PID must be ≥18 cm long.

mcqs.q: A rectangular PID (collimator) reduces patient exposure compared with a round one by about:
mcqs.explain: A rectangular PID limits the beam close to the receptor size, reducing exposure by 71–80%; a film holder reduces it by ~60%.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a benefit of beam collimation?
mcqs.explain: Collimation DECREASES patient exposure, scatter and film fog while increasing image quality — it never increases exposure.

mcqs.q: The federal minimum aluminium filtration for an intra-oral machine operating at 70 kVp is:
mcqs.explain: Minimum filtration is 1.5 mm Al at/below 70 kVp and 2 mm Al above 70 kVp — it removes long-wavelength, low-energy photons that only harm the patient.

mcqs.q: The position-distance rule for the operator during exposure is to stand:
opts: At least 6 ft (2 m) away, at 90°–135° to the beam
Right beside the tube head holding the film
Directly behind the patient in the beam path
Within 1 ft of the patient's head
mcqs.explain: The operator stands ≥6 ft away at 90°–135° to the primary beam (behind a barrier) and never holds the film or tube head.

mcqs.q: The lead thyroid collar and lead apron are used to:
opts: Shield the patient's radiosensitive tissues from scattered radiation
mcqs.explain: Lead aprons and thyroid collars are barriers that protect the patient's radiosensitive tissues (gonads, thyroid) from scattered radiation.

mcqs.q: A lead-FREE (Xenolite alloy) apron offers:
opts: The same protection as lead, but lighter and without lead-exposure risk
mcqs.explain: Xenolite alloy sheeting gives the same protection as conventional lead aprons without the heavy weight or risk of lead exposure.

mcqs.q: Dosimetry is defined as:
opts: Determining the unit of radiation exposure or dose received
mcqs.explain: Dosimetry is the measurement of radiation exposure/dose; methods include film badges, ionization chambers and thermoluminescent dosimeters.

mcqs.q: Thermoluminescent dosimetry (TLD) most commonly uses crystals of:
mcqs.explain: TLD uses LiF (and some CaF₂:Mn). Heating the irradiated crystal releases visible light proportional to absorbed energy; LiF's low atomic number mimics soft tissue.

mcqs.q: In a film badge, the amount of radiation exposure is determined by:
opts: The degree of darkening of the developed film
mcqs.explain: Film in a metal badge is processed and the degree of darkening indicates the exposure received over time — used to check radiation-safety practices.

mcqs.q: An ionization chamber measures exposure using:
opts: Charged collecting plates separated by air, connected to an electrometer
mcqs.explain: An ionization chamber is a pair of oppositely-charged plates separated by a standard volume of air, connected to an electrometer (e.g. the Victoreen condenser r-meter).

mcqs.q: Radiation dose limits are expressed in:
mcqs.explain: Annual dose limits are stated in milliSievert (mSv), the unit of effective/equivalent dose.

mcqs.q: Faster film reduces dose but its main trade-off is:
mcqs.explain: Faster films require less exposure (lower dose) but at the cost of a slight decrease in image quality (graininess).

mcqs.q: Deterministic effects are best prevented by:
opts: Accepting any dose since there is no threshold
mcqs.explain: Deterministic effects have a threshold; keeping doses below it prevents them. Stochastic effects (no threshold) are reduced to an acceptable level.

saqs.q: Name the three sources of radiation in dental radiology.
saqs.a: Primary beam (from the focal spot), leakage (from other tube parts), and secondary/scattered radiation (from matter the beam passes through).

saqs.q: State the ALARA principle and why it exists.
saqs.a: As Low As Reasonably Achievable — minimize exposure because no matter how small the dose, some stochastic effect may result (no threshold).

saqs.q: List four ways to reduce a patient's radiographic dose during the examination.
saqs.a: Fast film (D→E→F) / rare-earth screens; long FSFD (−32%); rectangular collimation (−71–80%); aluminium filtration (1.5–2 mm). Plus good patient selection & processing.

saqs.q: What is the minimum aluminium filtration required, and what does filtration achieve?
saqs.a: 1.5 mm Al ≤70 kVp, 2 mm Al >70 kVp. It removes long-wavelength, low-energy photons that only add to patient (skin) dose.
Operator stands ≥6 ft (2 m) from the patient at 90°–135° to the primary beam, behind a barrier, and never holds the film or tube.

saqs.q: Name the three methods of dosimetry.
Differentiate primary beam, leakage and scattered radiation in terms of patient vs operator dose.
saqs.a: Primary beam gives the diagnostic patient dose; scattered radiation (from the patient) is the main operator dose; leakage from the tube housing is minimized by shielding.
